prompt.context: De Beers, one of the leading diamond exploration companies in the world, is thinking about entering the retail business. De Beers is currently active in exploration, extraction, and distribution. They would like to enter retail but will NOT enter polishing or jewelling. Basically, De Beers wants to take advantage of their brand equity to sell finished diamonds (e.g. engagement rings). They would continue selling raw diamonds to polishers and would then buy finished diamonds from jewelers to sell in their own stores.
prompt.question: Should De Beers enter the retail business?

clarifying_info.q: What is De Beers' current position in the value chain?
clarifying_info.a: De Beers is currently in exploration, extraction, and distribution. The full value chain is: exploration – extraction – distribution – polishing and finishing – jewelers – retail.
The customers are wealthy individuals. The typical customers will likely be located in large metropolitan areas such as New York or London.
You can assume the industry is healthy and ignore competition for this analysis.

clarifying_info.q: Where will the store be located?
clarifying_info.a: The store will be located in London.

clarifying_info.q: What are the store's real estate costs?
clarifying_info.a: The store costs £300 per square meter per month and covers 5,000 square meters.

exhibits.shows: Interviewer instructions describing the sequence of questions: framework/value chain, fixed costs estimation (real estate), and gross margin calculation
exhibits.data: Store location: London; Rent: £300 per square meter per month; Store size: 5,000 square meters

exhibits.data: P1: Price £300, Gross Margin 20%; P2: Price £500, Gross Margin 30%; P3: Price £1,000, Gross Margin 10%; P4: Price £1,800, Gross Margin 20%; P5: Price £5,000, Gross Margin 30%

framework: Understand the value chain: exploration – extraction – distribution – polishing and finishing – jewelers – retail; De Beers enters only at the retail end
Business / Industry: assess industry health and competitive dynamics
Customers: identify target segment (wealthy individuals in major metros) and demand potential
Profits: break into Revenues (pricing structure, product mix) and Costs (fixed costs dominated by real estate, plus security, salaries, insurance, fixtures)
Feasibility: translate breakeven volume into a daily/hourly sales rate to stress-test viability

questions.prompt: What are the main fixed costs for a De Beers retail store, and what is the annual real estate cost for the London store?
questions.guidance: Candidate should brainstorm: real estate (rent), salaries, security, insurance, fixtures/displays. For the real estate calculation, candidate must recognize that store location and size drive the number. Interviewer provides: £300/m²/month and 5,000 m².

math.setup: Annual rent = price per square meter per month × store size × 12 months

questions.prompt: Calculate the profit per unit for each of the 5 products. Then determine how many diamonds De Beers must sell per year to break even.
questions.guidance: Interviewer reads out product prices and gross margin percentages; candidate calculates profit per unit = price × gross margin. Candidate then asks for allocation mix to compute a weighted average profit per diamond. Breakeven = Fixed Costs ÷ Weighted average profit per unit.

math.setup: Profit per unit = Price × Gross Margin %. Weighted average profit = sum of (Allocation Mix × Profit per unit). Breakeven units = Fixed costs ÷ Weighted average profit.

questions.prompt: Is it feasible to sell 60,000 diamonds per year in one London store?
questions.guidance: Candidate should decompose the annual target into smaller time units to evaluate feasibility. Strong answer converts annual to monthly, daily, and hourly rates, then judges whether that rate is realistic for a luxury diamond retailer.

math.setup: Break 60,000 diamonds/year into monthly, daily, and hourly rates.
steps: Assuming 20 working days per month: 5,000 ÷ 20 = 250 diamonds per day
Assuming store open 10 hours per day: 250 ÷ 10 = 25 diamonds per hour
math.answer: 25 diamonds per hour — clearly infeasible. Luxury diamond shoppers (e.g. engagement ring buyers) shop around extensively before purchasing, making a rate of 25 per hour per store unrealistic.

questions.prompt: Given that the breakeven is unachievable at current costs, what should De Beers do?
questions.guidance: Candidate must identify the biggest cost driver (real estate) and propose levers to reduce fixed costs or increase revenue per unit. Strong candidate mentions: (1) reduce store size — 5,000 m² is far too large for small items like diamonds; (2) explore other locations with lower rent; (3) focus the product mix on the most profitable items (P5 at 30% margin, P2 at 30% margin).

brainstorming.prompt: What fixed costs should De Beers anticipate for a retail diamond store?

categories.name: Real Estate
ideas: Rent (dominant cost driver — location and size critical)

categories.name: Inventory
ideas: Working capital for finished diamond inventory

recommendation: De Beers should re-think its retail strategy as currently structured. To break even, the London store must sell approximately 25 diamonds per hour, which is highly unlikely given the considered, high-involvement nature of luxury diamond purchases.
De Beers should first focus on dramatically reducing store size to lower the fixed cost base — 5,000 m² is far larger than necessary to display and sell small, high-value items like diamonds.
risks: Even a smaller store may struggle to generate sufficient foot traffic for high-frequency diamond sales
Brand dilution risk if the retail execution does not meet luxury standards
Potential channel conflict with existing jeweler partners who currently buy finished diamonds from De Beers
next_steps: Pilot with a significantly smaller store format (e.g. 200–500 m²) in a prime metropolitan location to lower fixed costs
Evaluate alternative high-traffic luxury locations (airport luxury corridors, high-end department store concessions) to reduce real estate burden
Consider focusing the product assortment on highest-margin SKUs (P2 at 30% and P5 at 30%) to maximize profit per unit sold
Assess partnership or concession models that reduce fixed cost exposure before committing to standalone flagship stores
